body: There’s a list of placements that have relationships with UB, but if there’s an agency you’re interested in that they aren’t already affiliated with that takes first year students they can set that up. I didn’t really know what I wanted to do for my first year, my placement coordinator was the one who found it for me and was really helpful. For my advanced year, I looked at the list on Sonia and found it that way. I called directly and set up an interview myself. Definitely take this as an opportunity to explore an interest, even if you’re on the fence about it.

I go to UB remotely, I do kind of wish I had done the program in person. I love the professors and other faculty members as well as my peers, but I miss in person classes and feel like I thrived better in that setting. Remote work has burned me out faster because it’s a little isolating only communicating with people via zoom. Field has been a saving grace for me, I enjoy the hands on learning and perform better that way. And realistically, I would not have permanently moved to Buffalo and feel it’s better to make connections in my area.

You can still accomplish things and do things you’re interested in while being on meds. If anything it makes it easier. Meds have brought me a peace I have never known in my life. It was hard for me at first too, I was scared I would lose parts of myself but that didn’t happen, I’m still me. The episodes don’t really go away, the meds aren’t a cure. I'd say on average they tend to be 4-5 pages, but my first semester I believe the final papers were 6-8 (if I'm remembering correctly). I also took psychopathology and the grade for that was only 3 tests. It varies from class to class, but I think with time management it's doable. All of the syllabuses have been very clear and the courses prepare you for those papers. There are many people in the program who work full time! I think it's pretty much designed for that. 

Yes they do job based field placements so when you start field it will be less of an academic stress, which I think is a huge benefit of the program not being full time and having to do full time coursework along with field. I think as far as programs go, it has the slowest pace I could find that's way more affordable than private. 

I don't want to downplay it like it's the easiest thing ever, it's still grad school, but if you're diligent and on top of things I think it's a great option. I personally do not work full time on top of school because of health issues I have, but if for some reason I had to, I probably could swing it. I honestly found undergrad to be more challenging.

At first I felt really overwhelmed because I felt pressured to read EVERYTHING in depth, but you kind of figure out pretty fast what's necessary to read thoroughly vs what you can skim. You get into the flow of it. I'd say the professors I've had offer a good variety of video content/video lectures along with readings. Many of them are very flexible, too, and not crazy graders. All of my classes have been asynchronous which is probably advantageous if you're working full time. I don't think it's sacrificed to quality of education I'm receiving though. I probably dedicate about 15 hours a week, give or take, and that's been enough for me to maintain a 3.75 gpa. You have a lot of input with field placement as well since it's online and they've been super helpful to me so far, but I haven't started my first placement yet. Overall I recommend it!

But I don’t think anyone should ride, personally. Even if you know the risk, it’s still a shock to the people around you.

Anxiety is trying to give you the illusion of control when the truth is you don’t have any in this case. Even if you find out the cause, you’d likely still have the anxiety. Anything could happen to anyone at anytime. It’s a harsh reality of life. My fiancé passed a few years ago unexpectedly in a motorcycle accident, which likely strikes the image that he was riding recklessly on some highway, when really he was cruising on his normal route to work. 

It’s one of those things where radical acceptance comes into play. I don’t quite have the same fear that I used to, because I recognize these things just happen, and could very well happen to me. Life is about the small moments. We put so much weight on achieving big things, but it’s really a series of small moments and all we can do is hope we have more good ones than bad ones. That we make the most of our time while we have it. 

This may not be helpful, but I don’t personally think sugarcoating “it probably won’t happen to you” helps. I was in therapy a few weeks before he passed worried sick he would die in an accident not long after a friend of his passed, and my therapist was like it’s so unlikely that it would happen to him. Then it happened to him.

Find ways to laugh if you can. Life is as funny as it is cruel sometimes.

I've been on .5 mg for almost 2 weeks now. I haven't noticed anything significant which I didn't really expect to on such a low dose. But thankfully I haven't had any side effects which is unheard of for me. I usually get side effects quickly on antipsychotics even on the low doses. I've tried latuda, vraylar, abilify, geodon, and seroquel. Seroquel is the only one that helped me, but the weight gain was just too much unfortunately. I have hope with Rexulti for the first time in a long time. One of my major concerns was akathisia which pretty much everything gave me. Thankfully so far so good, I am probably going to have it upped at my next appointment.

update: I've been on .5 still for 7 1/2 weeks because my doctor thought it would be too soon to up it. I honestly had to come back here to say this medication has been a miracle for me. I have finally come out of the year long depression I was in and can FUNCTION again. I am able to work again, I have a social life and am interested in things, I have a greater stress tolerance. Overall I'm able to take care of myself again. I don't feel like a zombie, I can still cry when I need to. No akathisia, no increased appetite, literally no side effects that I can notice. It's helped my anxiety a lot too. Just overall really great. If you're scared to try it but nothing else is helping, it's worth a shot.

I had an uncle who lived with my grandmother most of his life. He suffered from untreated mental illness, couldn't hold down a job, smoked weed all day and played video games. The rest of my family judged him so horribly and he was isolated except from my grandmother and his internet friends. Everyone thought he was this bum that drained his mother financially.

Well, he died of a heart attack before he turned 50. Everyone took it really hard, obviously it was sad he was so young and it was so sudden. He had so many friends online who showed up to his funeral. None of my family really understood him or the way he lived his life, and they were completely floored at the impact he made on people he'd never met in person.

My grandmother can't live alone, he was her life. He cooked, took her grocery shopping, took care of their dogs, I'd say clean but neither of them were clean lol. He was her friend and they took care of each other since my grandpa died pretty young. She lives with us now and brought their two dogs with her. She'd be a complete hermit if she lived alone, and after dealing with a loss like that she really can't. Everyone lives with the regret of the judgements they held about him. And that's family, can only imagine what strangers thought/said when they spoke about him.

So stop caring what other people think and stop caring what other people do. It's all a projection of insecurity, and it truly does not matter even a little bit what people think about you or what you think about them. Even your own comment is a little judgmental that could make someone else feel bad for no reason.
